Kollūru
------------------------------------------
Situated on the bank of the small river Sauparṇikā and at the foot of the Western Ghats, this small town is drawing very big crowds throughout the year, because of its famous temple of the goddess Mūkāmbikā. It is located at a distance of 147 kms. (90 miles) from Mangalore on the west coast in Karnataka State.
According to the local legends, it was originally known as Mahāraṇyapura. Since a famous sage, Kola महर्षि, practised austerities here to please the Divine मोथेर्, it was renamed Kolāpura. This name was gradually transformed into कोल्लूरु in the local language.
A fierce demon, Kaṁha or Mūkāsura by name, who had been terrorising the world, was killed by the देवी (the Divine मोथेर्) at this place. She decided to stay back here at the request of the sage, manifesting herself in the form of an udbhavaliṅga (self manifested शिवलिङ्ग). It is this लिङ्ग in the sanctum of the temple that is being worshipped even now. Its speciality is that it is divided into two unequal parts by a golden line, the larger part on the left representing the three aspects of the देवी (Mahākālī, महालक्ष्मी and Mahāsarasvatī) and the smaller part, the Hindu Trinity (Śiva, विष्णु and ब्रह्मा).
Śaṅkara (A.

-820) is said to have worshipped the goddess here. The beautiful metallic image of the deity was got made by him as per the vision he had had and installed.
It is in the seated posture with four hands. Two hands are holding the शङ्ख (conch) and the चक्र (discus). The other two are exhibiting the abhaya (protection) and varada (boon-giving) mudrās (hand-poses).
The entire process of rituals also was prescribed by शङ्कर.
The room near the sanctum of the देवी where he had had her vision, has been preserved and called शङ्कर-सिṁहासन.
The temple complex contains several subsidiary shrines dedicated to वीरभद्र (one of the terrific aspects of शिव), सुब्रह्मण्य, Pārtheśvara (Śiva), Pañcamukha-गणपति (with five faces), हनुमान्, Mahāviṣṇu and Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Worship to the main deity is performed three times per day: 5 A.M.; 11 A.M. and 7 P.M.
The western gate of the temple, through which शङ्कर is said to have entered, is normally kept closed and opened only on special occasions.
At a distance of 24 kms. (16 miles) from the town is the Koḍacādri (or Kuṭacādri) mountain, 1372 metres (4500 ft.) high. There is a thick forest on it as also a cave Citramūla (associated with शङ्कर) apart from a waterfall called Govindatīrtha.
Māraṇaghāṭ, the place where the demon Mūkāsura was beheaded by the देवी is in another direction. It has a temple with only a श्रीचक्र and no image.

Kolhāpur
------------------------------------------
Kolhāpur—formerly known as ‘Karavīra’—was the capital of the कोल्हापुर् State. Now it is a part of the State of Maharashtra. It is situated 240 kms. (150 miles) south of Pune, on the bank of the river Pañcagaṅgā.
It is one of the शक्तिपीठस् or Siddhapīṭhas with महालक्ष्मी as the chief presiding deity. This महालक्ष्मी is one of the three aspects of the देवी, described in the Devīmāhātmya or Durgāsaptaśatī.
The site of this city seems to be an ancient one since many Buddhist relics have been found in the archaeological excavations.
Out of the numerous temples, the shrines of महालक्ष्मी (also known as Ambābāī), Viṭhobā, Temblai, Mahākālī, Pratyaṅgiras and Yellamma are more famous.
Though the image of महालक्ष्मी is old, the present temple was perhaps built during the first quarter of the 18th century.
The shrine is like a cross, on plan and is surrounded by a spacious courtyard. The deity is facing west and hence the western gateway is the mahādvāra or the main entrance. There is a huge open hall called ‘Garuḍa-maṇṭapa’ constructed of wood, with square pillars and foliated arches. This has an image of गरुड facing the goddess.
The image of the goddess महालक्ष्मी has been carved out of black stone and is about 91 cms. (36 inches) in height. It is very beautiful. It has four arms holding गदा (mace), Mātuliṅga (a big fruit, similar to lemon in appearance), खेटक (shield) and pānapātra (bowl). On the crown of the देवी, are a शिवलिङ्ग and a cobra-hood. Standing behind the देवी is the lion, her वाहन or carrier.
There is also a sculptured श्रीचक्र or Śrīyantra on one of the walls of the temple in the मण्डप area.
The Navarātri festival, especially the Āśvina-śukla-pañcamī (the fifth day in the bright half of the month Āśvayuja or Āśvina, usually in September or October) is celebrated on a grand scale. The उत्सव-mūrti (processional image) is ceremonially carried in a procession through the city. On the pūrṇimā or full-मोओन् day of the same month, the temple door is decorated with lighted lamps.
There is a big bell also in the temple, which seems to have been obtained from the Portuguese.
Minor shrines housing Mahākālī and Mahāsarasvatī are also situated in the north and the south, in the same campus.
